name: Components
title: Resistors, capacitors, semiconductors and sensors
intro: Parts are how you build circuits. These lessons cover the everyday passives, then diodes, LEDs, a first look at BJT and MOSFET transistors, and a tour of common sensors. Values, symbols and one concrete use case matter more than memorising every variant.

lessons.title: Resistors
lessons.summary: Fixed resistors, ratings, and reading values.

sections.p: A resistor sets a known opposition to current. Carbon-film and metal-film through-hole parts are common on breadboards; chip resistors (0402, 0603, 0805…) dominate PCBs.
A 10 kΩ ±5% resistor can be about 9.5–10.5 kΩ. Metal-film 1% parts are cheap and preferred for dividers that need accuracy. Power rating (1/8 W, 1/4 W, 1 W…) limits heat.
Four-band code: digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance. Example: brown-black-orange-gold is 10 × 10³ Ω = 10 kΩ ±5%. When unsure, measure with a meter (power off).
Potentiometers are adjustable resistors. Thermistors change with temperature. LDRs change with light. Fusible resistors are meant to open safely under fault — not a toy.

lessons.title: Capacitors
lessons.summary: Storing charge, farads, and common types.

sections.p: A capacitor stores energy in an electric field between conductors separated by an insulator (dielectric). Capacitance C is in farads (F). Practical parts are µF, nF or pF. Q = C V for the charge on the plates.
Capacitors block steady DC once charged and pass changing signals. That is why they appear as coupling and decoupling parts. Bigger C stores more charge at the same voltage.
Ceramic (often MLCC) are small and non-polar. Electrolytic and tantalum are polar — reverse voltage can destroy them, sometimes violently. Film capacitors are common in analog audio and snubbers.
A 16 V electrolytic on a 12 V rail is common. Derate: do not run polar caps at the ragged edge of their voltage rating, especially with ripple and heat.

lessons.title: Inductors
lessons.summary: Magnetic storage, henries, and where you meet them.

sections.p: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field when current flows. Inductance L is in henries (H). Hobby parts are often µH or mH. Ideal relation: v = L di/dt — voltage appears when current tries to change.
Inductors resist sudden current change. They pass steady DC (apart from winding resistance) and impede high-frequency AC. That makes them useful in filters and switch-mode supplies.
Interrupt current in a coil (relay, motor) and the inductor makes a voltage spike. A flyback diode across a DC relay coil gives that current a safe path.
Coupled inductors make transformers: AC on a primary induces voltage on a secondary. DC alone on a quiet primary does not transfer power through an ideal transformer.

sections.p: A diode allows current easily in one direction (forward) and blocks the other (reverse), within ratings. Silicon signal diodes often drop about 0.6–0.7 V when forward conducting; Schottky diodes drop less (often ~0.2–0.4 V).
Power diodes turn AC into pulsing DC. A bridge rectifier uses four diodes. After rectification, capacitors smooth the result.
Watch forward current (e.g. 1 A) and reverse voltage (PIV / V_RRM). Exceed reverse voltage and the diode can avalanche or fail.
Zeners are used in reverse to hold an approximate voltage when current is limited by a resistor. They are for references and clamps, not heavy power regulation alone.

sections.p: An LED is a diode that emits light when forward current flows. Forward voltage depends on colour and chemistry: often ~1.8–2.2 V for red, ~3.0–3.3 V for blue/white. Always use a series resistor or a constant-current driver.
From 5 V to a 2 V red LED at 10 mA: R = (5 − 2) / 0.010 = 300 Ω → use 330 Ω. Too little resistance and the LED (or GPIO) dies; too much and it is simply dim.
Long lead / anode to the more positive side through the resistor; flat edge / cathode toward ground in many packages. If it does not light, check orientation before raising current.
Watt-class LEDs need heatsinks and proper drivers. Parallel LEDs without per-string control share current poorly. Series strings need enough voltage headroom.

sections.p: A BJT (bipolar junction transistor) has three terminals: collector, base, emitter (NPN) or emitter, base, collector (PNP). A small base current controls a larger collector current. Rough rule in active mode: I_C ≈ β I_B, with β often 50–300.
Emitter to ground, collector to the load then to +V, base driven through a resistor from a GPIO. When the base is driven, collector current lights a lamp or relay coil (add a flyback diode on coils).
As a switch, design for saturation: enough base current so V_CE is small (often <0.2 V). Rule of thumb: I_B ≈ I_C / 10 for switching, more conservative than β alone.
Watch V_CEO, I_C max, and power. BJTs drop more voltage than a good MOSFET switch at high current, so MOSFETs dominate many power switches — next lesson.

lessons.title: MOSFET transistors (intro)
lessons.summary: Voltage-controlled switches for loads and logic.

sections.p: A MOSFET uses a gate voltage to control current between drain and source. Gate current is tiny at DC (mostly charging capacitance). N-channel low-side switches are common: load from +V to drain, source to ground, gate driven from a GPIO or driver.
V_GS(th) is when the FET just begins to conduct — not when it is a good switch. For 3.3 V GPIO, pick a logic-level FET with low R_DS(on) at 3.3 V or 4.5 V on the datasheet graph.
When on, the FET looks like a small resistor. P ≈ I² R_DS(on). A 10 mΩ FET at 5 A dissipates about 0.25 W — still needs copper and sometimes a heatsink at higher current.
Gates are ESD-sensitive. A gate-source resistor (e.g. 100 kΩ) keeps the FET off if the driver floats. Gate resistors (10–100 Ω) can tame ringing with long wires.

lessons.title: Sensors overview
lessons.summary: Turning physical quantities into voltages, currents or bits.

sections.p: Sensors convert temperature, light, motion, distance, chemistry and more into electrical signals. Some are analog (a voltage you measure with an ADC); some are digital (I²C/SPI words or a simple high/low pin).
A potentiometer is a position sensor. A photoresistor divider senses light. Many thermistor circuits are dividers into an ADC. Scale and noise matter: add filtering and calibration.
DHT-style humidity modules spit serial bits. IMUs report acceleration over SPI/I²C. A PIR motion module often gives a simple digital alarm pin.

Match voltages (3.3 V sensor on a 5 V ADC needs care). Provide clean decoupling. Do not share noisy motor grounds carelessly with microvolt sensor returns. Read the absolute maximum ratings before wiring.
A raw ADC count is not "°C" until you apply a transfer function and calibration. Datasheets give typical curves; real parts need checking.

lessons.title: Switches, buzzers and connectors
lessons.summary: The mechanical and interconnect parts every bench needs.

sections.p: Not every part is a semiconductor. Switches, buttons, connectors, speakers/buzzers and relays show up in almost every project.
A push-button with a pull-up reads low when pressed. Mechanical contacts bounce: the signal chatters for milliseconds. Debounce in software or with a small RC / logic.
A relay is an electrically controlled switch. Coil side is low voltage; contact side might be a different circuit — still respect isolation and ratings. Use a flyback diode on DC coils.
USB, barrel jacks, pin headers, screw terminals: each has current and mating-cycle limits. Strain-relief wires so the solder joint is not the hinge.
Magnetic buzzers may need a driver transistor. Piezo elements are mostly capacitive loads — drive them with care and do not expect huge bass from a tiny disc.
